analysis.one_liner: Cuts student loan fees and interest rates, allows consolidation loan refinancing, and raises Pell Grants to $7,000.
analysis.headline: The bill never left committee; it was referred to the House Education Committee and a subcommittee in April 2005 and received no further action, no markup, and no vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would let borrowers refinance federally guaranteed student consolidation loans, lower the cap on consolidation loan interest rates to 6.8%, end the origination fees that lenders and the Education Department charge borrowers on new loans, and raise the maximum Pell Grant to $7,000 for the 2006-07 school year and four years after, locking in a higher grant instead of the current fixed amount [S2][S3]. Together these changes would cut the total cost of borrowing for millions of current and future students and put more grant money in place of loans for low-income students [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Student loan borrowers and low-income college students gain most. Refinancing would let borrowers who consolidated loans during the short window when higher rates applied trade them in for cheaper ones [S3]. Eliminating origination fees—typically up to 4% of the loan principal in the Direct Loan program—would immediately shave hundreds of dollars off the cost of every new federal loan [S3]. The higher $7,000 Pell maximum would reduce how much low-income students have to borrow or pay out of pocket [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: Removes the legal prohibition on refinancing federal student consolidation loans, letting borrowers who are stuck with older, higher-rate consolidation loans trade them in at the current low rate [S2][S3].
Cuts the statutory cap on the interest rate for consolidation loans to 6.8%, limiting how much lenders can charge on refinanced loans [S2][S3].

Prohibits lenders and the Education Department from charging borrowers any origination fee on new federal loans—up to 4% of principal under Direct Loans—starting the first July 1 after enactment [S2][S3].
Raises the maximum Pell Grant to $7,000 for academic year 2006-07 and the four following years, increasing need-based aid that does not have to be repaid [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Lenders in the federally guaranteed (FFEL) loan program would lose the origination fee income the bill bans and would face competition from borrowers refinancing older loans [S3]. The federal Treasury would bear the cost of larger Pell Grants and the interest-rate savings, which would otherwise come from loan interest and fees paid by borrowers [S2][S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: FFEL lenders and the federal Treasury

drawbacks.text: Ending origination fees and cutting interest rate caps reduces federal loan program revenue, so the cost must be covered by appropriations or by shrinking other loan program subsidies; the bill's text does not show how the Pell increase is funded [S3].

Raising the Pell maximum for six consecutive years is a large, permanent federal spending commitment—at the time the maximum grant was around $4,050—so the price tag for taxpayers would be in the billions of dollars annually [S3].

Allowing refinancing of consolidation loans creates a repeated refinancing incentive that lenders argued would make the consolidation program more expensive and less predictable to guarantee, a cost that can be passed back into the program.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits to borrowers are concrete and large: several hundred dollars saved per loan in fees alone, relief for borrowers stuck in older high-rate consolidations, and thousands of dollars more in need-based grants. The honest cost is that the federal government gives up fee and interest revenue and picks up a multi-billion-dollar annual Pell obligation. As a transfer from the Treasury and lenders to students, the trade is favorable to ordinary people, but the bill's lack of an offset means the spending question was legitimately open.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee and then to a subcommittee, and no committee or floor action ever followed before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on March 16, 2005 and referred the same day to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce [S5].
On April 18, 2005 it was referred to the Subcommittee on 21st Century Competitiveness, which is where the record ends [S5].
The bill had 29 cosponsors, 28 Democrats and 1 Republican [S4].
No markup, hearing, committee vote, or floor action is recorded for the bill during the remainder of the 109th Congress [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Guaranteed student loan lenders kept the origination fee revenue and the prohibition on refinancing consolidation loans intact for another two years, and the Treasury was spared the cost of the higher Pell Grants. Borrowers who were paying origination fees and stuck in older high-rate consolidation loans paid the cost of the delay.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Student loan lenders kept fees and high-rate loans

for.name: Rep. Rosa DeLauro
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to cut student loan fees, allow consolidation loan refinancing, and raise the Pell Grant maximum.

for.name: 28 House Democrats and 1 House Republican
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it bipartisan sponsorship but far short of the majority needed to force committee action.

against.name: Rep. John Boehner
against.role: Chair, House Committee on Education and the Workforce
against.what_they_did: As committee chair, never scheduled a markup or committee vote on the bill; it sat in subcommittee referral with no further action for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Support was almost entirely Democratic—28 of 29 cosponsors—with a single Republican cosponsor, and the Republican-controlled committee never acted on it.

industries.industry: FFEL student loan lenders and guaranty agencies
industries.note: The bill would ban origination fees on new guaranteed loans and allow borrowers to refinance consolidation loans at a rate capped at 6.8%, directly cutting lender fee income and marketable loan volume. Lenders' interest in keeping fees and the refinancing ban ran against borrowers' interest in cheaper loans [S3].

industries.industry: Federal student loan program (Direct Loan side of the Education Department)
industries.note: The Department would lose the 4% origination fee it charges Direct Loan borrowers, but the Pell increase flows as federal spending rather than through an industry. Borrowers gain on both counts [S3].
